claim: The coding sequence of mEos4b was inserted in exon 2 of the Glrb gene by homologous recombination supported by a guide RNA (CRISPR-Cas9).
source: The coding sequence of mEos4b was inserted in exon 2 of the Glrb gene by homologous recombination supported by a guide RNA (CRISPR-Cas9) to increase recombination efficiency (ICS, Illkirch, France).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method used to generate the knock-in mouse model.

claim: The fluorophore sequence was inserted after the signal peptide and before the N-terminus of the mature GlyRβ subunit.
source: Specifically, the fluorophore sequence was inserted after the signal peptide and before the N-terminus of the mature GlyRβ subunit, meaning that it does not interrupt the coding sequence of the receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the insertion site and references a figure showing the construct design.

claim: The correct insertion was confirmed by amplification and sequencing of genomic DNA.
source: The correct insertion was confirmed by amplification and sequencing of genomic DNA.
evidence: The manuscript describes the validation method used.

claim: Equal concentrations of GlrbEos and wild-type (WT) transcript (GlrbWT) are expressed in heterozygous animals.
source: Semi-quantitative RT-PCR revealed that equal concentrations of GlrbEos and the wild-type (WT) transcript (GlrbWT) are expressed in heterozygous animals.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from semi-quantitative RT-PCR experiments.

claim: KI animals follow Mendelian inheritance when bred to homozygosity.
source: When bred to homozygosity, KI animals follow Mendelian inheritance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), exhibit normal lifespans (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and display no overt phenotype, suggesting that the GlyR expression and/or function are not altered.
evidence: The manuscript reports breeding data shown in a figure.

claim: Homozygous KI animals exhibit normal lifespans.
source: When bred to homozygosity, KI animals follow Mendelian inheritance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), exhibit normal lifespans (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and display no overt phenotype, suggesting that the GlyR expression and/or function are not altered.
evidence: The manuscript reports survival data shown in a figure.

claim: Homozygous KI animals display no overt phenotype.
source: When bred to homozygosity, KI animals follow Mendelian inheritance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), exhibit normal lifespans (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and display no overt phenotype, suggesting that the GlyR expression and/or function are not altered.
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data about the animals.

claim: The maximal chloride currents at saturating glycine concentrations of 300 μM were not significantly different in GlrbEos/Eos animals.
source: The maximal chloride currents at saturating glycine concentrations of 300 μM were not significantly different in GlrbEos/Eos animals, despite a minor increase in the EC50 (GlrbWT/WT 100 ± 5 μM, GlrbEos/Eos 130 ± 9 μM, p=0.0123 t-test).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological measurements comparing WT and KI animals.

claim: GlrbEos/Eos animals show a minor increase in the EC50 compared to wild-type (GlrbWT/WT 100 ± 5 μM, GlrbEos/Eos 130 ± 9 μM, p=0.0123 t-test).
source: The maximal chloride currents at saturating glycine concentrations of 300 μM were not significantly different in GlrbEos/Eos animals, despite a minor increase in the EC50 (GlrbWT/WT 100 ± 5 μM, GlrbEos/Eos 130 ± 9 μM, p=0.0123 t-test).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: The presence of the N-terminal fluorophore does not affect GlyR function under physiological conditions.
source: In view of the millimolar concentration of glycine present during synaptic transmission (Beato, 2008; Legendre, 1998), these data indicate that the presence of the N-terminal fluorophore does not affect GlyR function under physiological conditions.
evidence: The manuscript interprets electrophysiological data in the context of cited literature about physiological glycine concentrations.

claim: Hill coefficients for GlrbWT/WT and GlrbEos/Eos were in the range of 3.5–4.
source: Hill coefficients for GlrbWT/WT and GlrbEos/Eos were in the range of 3.5–4, arguing for cooperativity of the subunits during glycine binding.
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated Hill coefficients from electrophysiological data.

claim: Hill coefficients in the range of 3.5–4 argue for cooperativity of the subunits during glycine binding.
source: Hill coefficients for GlrbWT/WT and GlrbEos/Eos were in the range of 3.5–4, arguing for cooperativity of the subunits during glycine binding.
evidence: The manuscript interprets Hill coefficient data in terms of receptor cooperativity.

claim: The glycinergic origin of the chloride influx was confirmed by blocking the currents recorded in the presence of 100 μM glycine with 10 μM strychnine.
source: The glycinergic origin of the chloride influx was confirmed by blocking the currents recorded in the presence of 100 μM glycine with 10 μM strychnine.
evidence: The manuscript reports a pharmacological control experiment.

claim: mEos4b-GlyRβ was widely expressed at inhibitory synapses in the thalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla.
source: Indeed, mEos4b-GlyRβ was widely expressed at inhibitory synapses in the thalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports confocal imaging observations across brain regions.

claim: Very little fluorescence was detected in the forebrain despite the high reported expression of the Glrb transcript.
source: Very little fluorescence was detected in the forebrain despite the high reported expression of the Glrb transcript (Fujita et al., 1991; Malosio et al., 1991), suggesting that protein levels are controlled by post-transcriptional mechanisms in a region-specific manner, as previously proposed (Weltzien et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging observations and cites literature about transcript expression.

claim: Protein levels are controlled by post-transcriptional mechanisms in a region-specific manner.
source: Very little fluorescence was detected in the forebrain despite the high reported expression of the Glrb transcript (Fujita et al., 1991; Malosio et al., 1991), suggesting that protein levels are controlled by post-transcriptional mechanisms in a region-specific manner, as previously proposed (Weltzien et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript infers post-transcriptional control based on the discrepancy between transcript and protein levels, citing a previous proposal.

claim: The integrated mEos4b intensity at gephyrin-positive ventral horn synapses was exactly two times higher in GlrbEos/Eos mice than in GlrbEos/WT.
source: The integrated mEos4b intensity at gephyrin-positive ventral horn synapses was exactly two times higher in GlrbEos/Eos mice than in GlrbEos/WT, demonstrating that both alleles are expressed with the same efficiency, and that the mEos4b fluorophore does not affect the synaptic localization of the receptor complexes.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative confocal imaging measurements.

claim: Both alleles are expressed with the same efficiency.
source: The integrated mEos4b intensity at gephyrin-positive ventral horn synapses was exactly two times higher in GlrbEos/Eos mice than in GlrbEos/WT, demonstrating that both alleles are expressed with the same efficiency, and that the mEos4b fluorophore does not affect the synaptic localization of the receptor complexes.
evidence: The manuscript infers equal allelic expression from the 2:1 intensity ratio.

claim: The mEos4b fluorophore does not affect the synaptic localization of the receptor complexes.
source: The integrated mEos4b intensity at gephyrin-positive ventral horn synapses was exactly two times higher in GlrbEos/Eos mice than in GlrbEos/WT, demonstrating that both alleles are expressed with the same efficiency, and that the mEos4b fluorophore does not affect the synaptic localization of the receptor complexes.
evidence: The manuscript infers normal synaptic localization from the proportional intensity increase.

claim: The intensity of synaptic mEos4b-GlyRβ puncta increased from dorsal to ventral both in homozygous and in heterozygous animals.
source: Across the spinal cord slices, the intensity of synaptic mEos4b-GlyRβ puncta increased from dorsal to ventral both in homozygous (Figure 1D and E) and in heterozygous animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative confocal imaging measurements across spinal cord regions.

claim: mRFP-gephyrin fluorescence was higher and more variable in the ventral horn.
source: Similarly, mRFP-gephyrin fluorescence was higher and more variable in the ventral horn, suggesting that synapses were on average about twice as big as those in the dorsal horn, despite being fewer in number (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports confocal imaging observations.

claim: Synapses in the ventral horn were on average about twice as big as those in the dorsal horn.
source: Similarly, mRFP-gephyrin fluorescence was higher and more variable in the ventral horn, suggesting that synapses were on average about twice as big as those in the dorsal horn, despite being fewer in number (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript infers synapse size from gephyrin fluorescence intensity.

claim: Ventral horn synapses were fewer in number than dorsal horn synapses.
source: Similarly, mRFP-gephyrin fluorescence was higher and more variable in the ventral horn, suggesting that synapses were on average about twice as big as those in the dorsal horn, despite being fewer in number (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports synapse counts from confocal imaging.

claim: The mEos4b/mRFP ratio was relatively equal across the spinal cord with the exception of the superficial layers of the dorsal horn.
source: The mEos4b/mRFP ratio was relatively equal across the spinal cord with the exception of the superficial layers of the dorsal horn, where GlyR levels were largely exceeded by gephyrin (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of the ratio of two fluorescent signals.

claim: In the superficial layers of the dorsal horn, GlyR levels were largely exceeded by gephyrin.
source: The mEos4b/mRFP ratio was relatively equal across the spinal cord with the exception of the superficial layers of the dorsal horn, where GlyR levels were largely exceeded by gephyrin (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of fluorescence ratios.

claim: The lower GlyR-scaffold occupancy of synapses in laminae I–III can be explained by the predominant expression of GABAARs that compete for receptor binding sites at these mixed inhibitory synapses.
source: The lower GlyR-scaffold occupancy of synapses in laminae I–III can be explained by the predominant expression of GABAARs that compete for receptor binding sites at these mixed inhibitory synapses (Alvarez et al., 1996; Lorenzo et al., 2014; Todd et al., 1996).
evidence: The manuscript explains the observation by citing literature about GABAAR expression in these regions.

claim: The spatial resolution of SRRF was 46 nm.
source: According to this analysis, the spatial resolution of SRRF was 46 nm and that of PALM 21 nm.
evidence: The manuscript reports resolution measurements using Fourier ring correlation.

claim: The spatial resolution of PALM was 21 nm.
source: According to this analysis, the spatial resolution of SRRF was 46 nm and that of PALM 21 nm.
evidence: The manuscript reports resolution measurements using Fourier ring correlation.

claim: The majority of synaptic clusters in the dual super-resolution images were small and spherical or elongated.
source: The majority of synaptic clusters in the dual super-resolution images were small and spherical or elongated.
evidence: The manuscript describes morphological observations from super-resolution imaging.

claim: Larger clusters displayed a variety of morphologies including elongated shapes seen in side view as well as convoluted structures.
source: Larger clusters displayed a variety of morphologies including elongated shapes seen in side view (Figure 2B) as well as convoluted structures, and were more frequently observed in the ventral horn (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes morphological observations from super-resolution imaging.

claim: Larger clusters were more frequently observed in the ventral horn.
source: Larger clusters displayed a variety of morphologies including elongated shapes seen in side view (Figure 2B) as well as convoluted structures, and were more frequently observed in the ventral horn (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative observations from super-resolution imaging.

claim: All mEos4b-GlyR clusters closely matched the mRFP-gephyrin clusters.
source: All mEos4b-GlyR clusters closely matched the mRFP-gephyrin clusters, confirming the localization of the receptors in the postsynaptic membrane.
evidence: The manuscript reports co-localization analysis from super-resolution imaging.

claim: The degree of co-localization of mEos4b-GlyRβ and mRFP-gephyrin was very high, with mean intensity correlation quotients (ICQ) around 0.3.
source: As expected of two directly interacting synaptic components, the degree of co-localization of mEos4b-GlyRβ and mRFP-gephyrin was very high, with mean intensity correlation quotients (ICQ) around 0.3 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), a value indicative of close spatial correlation (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative co-localization measurements and cites the method.

claim: An ICQ value of 0.3 is indicative of close spatial correlation.
source: As expected of two directly interacting synaptic components, the degree of co-localization of mEos4b-GlyRβ and mRFP-gephyrin was very high, with mean intensity correlation quotients (ICQ) around 0.3 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), a value indicative of close spatial correlation (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature to interpret the ICQ value.

claim: There were no obvious differences between the ICQ values of dorsal versus ventral synapses (0.28–0.3).
source: There were no obvious differences between the ICQ values of dorsal versus ventral synapses (0.28–0.3), indicating equivalent GlyRβ-gephyrin binding in the two regions.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative co-localization measurements.

claim: The amounts of receptor and scaffold proteins are closely correlated.
source: Quantitative comparison of mEos4b-GlyRβ and mRFP-gephyrin intensities confirmed that the amounts of receptor and scaffold proteins are closely correlated, and that the occupancy of receptor binding sites is the same in the dorsal and ventral horn, independent of synapse size (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensities.

claim: The occupancy of receptor binding sites is the same in the dorsal and ventral horn, independent of synapse size.
source: Quantitative comparison of mEos4b-GlyRβ and mRFP-gephyrin intensities confirmed that the amounts of receptor and scaffold proteins are closely correlated, and that the occupancy of receptor binding sites is the same in the dorsal and ventral horn, independent of synapse size (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of receptor-scaffold occupancy.

claim: The mean synapse area in the ventral horn was larger and more variable than in the dorsal region, both in animals of 2 and 10 months of age.
source: The mean synapse area in the ventral horn was larger and more variable than in the dorsal region, both in animals of 2 and 10 months of age (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of synapse area from PALM imaging.

claim: The overall number of synapses in ventral horn tissue was lower compared to the dorsal horn, significantly so by 10 months.
source: We also remarked that the overall number of synapses in ventral horn tissue was lower compared to the dorsal horn, significantly so by 10 months (Figure 2G; see also Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative synapse counts with statistical analysis.

claim: The inverse relationship between synapse number and size is likely due to the presence of different cell types in the two regions, specifically Renshaw cells and large motor neurons in the ventral horn that require strong inhibitory control.
source: The inverse relationship between synapse number and size is likely due to the presence of different cell types in the two regions, specifically Renshaw cells and large motor neurons in the ventral horn that require strong inhibitory control (e.g., Bhumbra et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript infers the reason for the observation based on known cell types and cites supporting literature.

claim: A median copy number of 114 pentameric GlyR complexes was calculated at dorsal horn synapses in 2-month-old animals.
source: We calculated a median copy number of 114 pentameric GlyR complexes at dorsal horn synapses and twice that number at ventral horn synapses in 2-month-old animals (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative molecule counting from PALM data.

claim: Ventral horn synapses have twice the number of GlyR complexes compared to dorsal horn synapses in 2-month-old animals.
source: We calculated a median copy number of 114 pentameric GlyR complexes at dorsal horn synapses and twice that number at ventral horn synapses in 2-month-old animals (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative molecule counting from PALM data.

claim: Copy numbers were almost identical at 10 months.
source: Copy numbers were almost identical at 10 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating that the glycinergic network was mature at both time points.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative molecule counting from PALM data at different ages.

claim: The glycinergic network was mature at both 2 and 10 months.
source: Copy numbers were almost identical at 10 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating that the glycinergic network was mature at both time points.
evidence: The manuscript infers network maturity from the stability of receptor copy numbers.

claim: Estimates from electrophysiological recordings in newborn, juvenile, and adult rat spinal cord neurons suggest the activation of as few as 7 and up to about 110 GlyRs during an average miniature inhibitory postsynaptic current (mIPSC).
source: These numbers exceed estimates derived from electrophysiological recordings in newborn, juvenile, and adult rat spinal cord neurons that suggest the activation of as few as 7 and up to about 110 GlyRs during an average miniature inhibitory postsynaptic current (mIPSC) (Chéry and de Koninck, 1999; Oleskevich et al., 1999; Singer and Berger, 1999; Takahashi, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature reporting electrophysiological estimates.

claim: The high numbers of GlyRs measured by fluorophore counting imply that the available receptors are not saturated by quantal release.
source: The high numbers of GlyRs measured by fluorophore counting therefore imply that the available receptors are not saturated by quantal release, which is likely to increase the dynamic range of postsynaptic inhibition (Alvarez, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript infers receptor saturation status from the comparison of counted receptors and electrophysiological estimates, citing supporting literature.

claim: Differences in receptor numbers result from differences in synapse size.
source: Our quantitative PALM data further demonstrate that differences in receptor numbers result from differences in synapse size (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of the relationship between receptor numbers and synapse size.

claim: Mean GlyR densities are ~2000 µm–2.
source: By combining the two parameters, we derived mean GlyR densities of ~2000 µm–2 (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated receptor densities from PALM data.

claim: Similar receptor densities of 1250 µm–2 and ~2000 µm–2 have been measured at GABAergic synapses in cerebellar stellate cells and in cultured hippocampal neurons, respectively.
source: Similar receptor densities of 1250 µm–2 and ~2000 µm–2 have been measured at GABAergic synapses in cerebellar stellate cells and in cultured hippocampal neurons, respectively (Liu et al., 2020; Nusser et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature reporting receptor densities at other inhibitory synapses.

claim: There were no differences in the GlyR packing density at dorsal and ventral horn synapses.
source: We saw no differences in the GlyR packing density at dorsal and ventral horn synapses, nor did we find a clear size dependence, as determined by linear regression of all synapses (Figure 2I) and the evolution of the coefficient of variation of GlyR density with respect to synapse area (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of receptor density across regions.

claim: There was no clear size dependence of GlyR packing density.
source: We saw no differences in the GlyR packing density at dorsal and ventral horn synapses, nor did we find a clear size dependence, as determined by linear regression of all synapses (Figure 2I) and the evolution of the coefficient of variation of GlyR density with respect to synapse area (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of the relationship between density and synapse size.

claim: GlyR density is constant and largely independent of neuron type, embryonic origin, or physiological function.
source: These findings are significant because they indicate that GlyR density is constant and largely independent of neuron type, embryonic origin, or physiological function.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the data on constant density across different synapse types.

claim: Assuming that gephyrin molecules are clustered at densities of up to 9000 µm–2, close to 50% of the receptor binding sites are occupied by GlyRs at native spinal cord synapses.
source: Assuming that gephyrin molecules are clustered at densities of up to 9000 µm–2 (Specht et al., 2013), our data also suggest that close to 50% of the receptor binding sites are occupied by GlyRs at native spinal cord synapses, in line with earlier observations of GlyR subunits that were overexpressed in cultured neurons (Patrizio et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript calculates receptor occupancy based on measured GlyR density and cited gephyrin density.

claim: All of the synapses that were both imaged by PALM and reconstructed with EM were functionally mature as judged by the apposition of a single presynaptic terminal containing synaptic vesicles.
source: All of the synapses that were both imaged by PALM and reconstructed with EM were functionally mature as judged by the apposition of a single presynaptic terminal containing synaptic vesicles.
evidence: The manuscript reports morphological observations from electron microscopy.

claim: Glycinergic synapses in the ventral horn were substantially larger and more variable in size than those in the dorsal horn.
source: In line with our PALM data, we found that glycinergic synapses in the ventral horn were substantially larger and more variable in size than those in the dorsal horn (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements from EM reconstructions.

claim: There was good correspondence between the calculated synapse areas in the EM and PALM image reconstructions.
source: There was good correspondence between the calculated synapse areas in the EM and PALM image reconstructions, even though PALM underestimated the sizes of some large ventral horn synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of measurements from two different imaging modalities.

claim: PALM underestimated the sizes of some large ventral horn synapses.
source: There was good correspondence between the calculated synapse areas in the EM and PALM image reconstructions, even though PALM underestimated the sizes of some large ventral horn synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of measurements from two different imaging modalities.

claim: PALM underestimation of large ventral synapse sizes is probably due to the fact that a majority of synapses are tilted, and that the axial component of the area is not captured in the SMLM projections.
source: This is probably due to the fact that a majority of synapses are tilted, and that the axial component of the area is not captured in the SMLM projections.
evidence: The manuscript infers the reason for the underestimation based on the imaging geometry.

claim: Most synapses in the dorsal horn were macular.
source: Whereas most synapses in the dorsal horn were macular, ventral synapses were frequently composed of subdomains (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: The manuscript reports morphological observations from EM reconstructions.

claim: Ventral synapses were frequently composed of subdomains.
source: Whereas most synapses in the dorsal horn were macular, ventral synapses were frequently composed of subdomains (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: The manuscript reports morphological observations from EM reconstructions.

claim: The degree of complexity scales with the size of the postsynaptic specialization.
source: In agreement with earlier studies (Alvarez et al., 1997; Lushnikova et al., 2011; Santuy et al., 2018), the degree of complexity scales with the size of the postsynaptic specialization (Figure 3F), and was taken into account for the calculation of the combined area in the EM serial sections.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of synapse morphology and cites supporting literature.

claim: Average receptor densities were approximately 2000 µm–2 based on the ratio of GlyR copy numbers and the area of the inhibitory postsynaptic specialization obtained by EM.
source: The ratio of GlyR copy numbers and the area of the inhibitory postsynaptic specialization obtained by EM resulted in average receptor densities of approximately 2000 µm–2 (Figure 3H).
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated receptor densities from combined PALM and EM data.

claim: There were no significant differences in receptor densities between synapses in the dorsal and the ventral horn.
source: Consistent with our PALM estimates, we did not observe significant differences between synapses in the dorsal and the ventral horn (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of receptor densities from EM-based measurements.

claim: The GlyR packing density was not dependent on synapse size.
source: Furthermore, the GlyR packing density was not dependent on synapse size (Figure 3I), supporting an earlier proposal (Lim et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis and cites supporting literature.

claim: GlyRs are assembled in a systematic manner, where receptor numbers increase linearly with synapse size.
source: This suggests that GlyRs are assembled in a systematic manner, where receptor numbers increase linearly with synapse size.
evidence: The manuscript infers the assembly principle from the constant density observation.

claim: GlyR occupancy at individual subdomains of the postsynaptic sites is uniform.
source: Since the morphological complexity of synapses increases with size, it can also be concluded that GlyR occupancy at individual subdomains of the postsynaptic sites is uniform.
evidence: The manuscript infers uniform occupancy from the constant density despite increasing complexity.

claim: GlyR densities were not significantly different within subclusters of reconstructed synapses.
source: GlyR densities were indeed not significantly different within subclusters of reconstructed synapses (Figure 3G and I, black data points).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of receptor density within subsynaptic domains.

claim: These findings point to a tight regulation of the architecture of glycinergic synapses across different molecular length scales, where GlyRs are arranged in sub-synaptic signaling units.
source: Together, these findings point to a tight regulation of the architecture of glycinergic synapses across different molecular length scales, where GlyRs are arranged in sub-synaptic signaling units.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the data on uniform density and subdomains.

claim: The mouse mutation oscillator (Glra1spd-ot/spd-ot) is recessively inherited.
source: The mouse mutation oscillator (Glra1spd-ot/spd-ot) is recessively inherited and causes a microdeletion and frameshift in the TM3-4 intracellular loop of the GlyRα1 subunit, leading to subunit truncation and subsequent loss of functional GlyRs at synapses (Kling et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing the oscillator mutation.

claim: The oscillator mutation causes a microdeletion and frameshift in the TM3-4 intracellular loop of the GlyRα1 subunit.
source: The mouse mutation oscillator (Glra1spd-ot/spd-ot) is recessively inherited and causes a microdeletion and frameshift in the TM3-4 intracellular loop of the GlyRα1 subunit, leading to subunit truncation and subsequent loss of functional GlyRs at synapses (Kling et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing the molecular nature of the mutation.

claim: The oscillator mutation leads to subunit truncation and subsequent loss of functional GlyRs at synapses.
source: The mouse mutation oscillator (Glra1spd-ot/spd-ot) is recessively inherited and causes a microdeletion and frameshift in the TM3-4 intracellular loop of the GlyRα1 subunit, leading to subunit truncation and subsequent loss of functional GlyRs at synapses (Kling et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing the functional consequences of the mutation.

claim: Homozygous oscillator mice do not live past 3 weeks of age.
source: Homozygous oscillator mice do not live past 3 weeks of age (Buckwalter et al., 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature reporting the survival of homozygous oscillator mice.

claim: Heterozygous oscillator animals have a normal lifespan.
source: In contrast, heterozygous animals have a normal lifespan and exhibit a more subtle phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data about heterozygous oscillator mice.

claim: Glra1spd-ot/WT mice display an increased startle reflex.
source: Glra1spd-ot/WT mice display an increased startle reflex and lower GlyRα1 levels (Kling et al., 1997), making them a suitable model for human hyperekplexia.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing the phenotype of heterozygous oscillator mice.

claim: Glra1spd-ot/WT mice have lower GlyRα1 levels.
source: Glra1spd-ot/WT mice display an increased startle reflex and lower GlyRα1 levels (Kling et al., 1997), making them a suitable model for human hyperekplexia.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing the molecular phenotype of heterozygous oscillator mice.

claim: The intensity of synaptic mEos4b-GlyRβ puncta in heterozygous oscillator animals was substantially lower than those of WT littermates.
source: The intensity of synaptic mEos4b-GlyRβ puncta in heterozygous oscillator animals was substantially lower than those of WT littermates, which explains the reductions in membrane levels of GlyR and gephyrin previously observed by Western blotting (Kling et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript reports confocal imaging measurements in oscillator mice and cites supporting literature.

claim: The number of gephyrin-positive synapses across the spinal cord remained unchanged between WT and oscillator.
source: The number of gephyrin-positive synapses across the spinal cord remained unchanged between WT and oscillator.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative synapse counts in oscillator and WT mice.

claim: The mean synapse area in the ventral horn was significantly larger than in the dorsal region in WT animals.
source: The mean synapse area in the ventral horn was significantly larger than in the dorsal region in WT animals (Figure 5B), in agreement with our earlier data (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of synapse area in WT animals.

claim: The difference in synapse area between dorsal and ventral horn was lost in Glra1spd-ot/WT littermates.
source: However, this difference was lost in Glra1spd-ot/WT littermates.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements of synapse area in oscillator mice.

claim: The overall number of synapses was lower in ventral horn tissue compared to the dorsal horn in both WT and oscillator animals.
source: The overall number of synapses was lower in ventral horn tissue compared to the dorsal horn in both WT and oscillator animals (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative synapse counts in both genotypes.

claim: The decrease in functional receptors in heterozygous oscillator mice manifests itself as a reduction in the size of ventral synapses.
source: These data suggest that the decrease in functional receptors in heterozygous oscillator mice manifests itself as a reduction in the size of ventral synapses.
evidence: The manuscript infers the manifestation of receptor loss from the synapse size measurements.

claim: The number and distribution of receptors in WT mice matched that of 2- and 10-month-old WT animals analyzed previously.
source: We further quantified the total number of endogenous GlyRs at synapses (Figure 5D) and found that the number and distribution of receptors in WT mice matched that of 2- and 10-month-old WT animals analyzed previously (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative molecule counting and compares across experiments.

claim: Similar copy numbers were found in dorsal synapses of heterozygous oscillator mice compared to WT littermates.
source: We found similar copy numbers in dorsal synapses of heterozygous oscillator mice compared to WT littermates.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative molecule counting in oscillator and WT mice.

claim: In ventral tissue, there was a shift towards lower receptor numbers per synapse in oscillator mice.
source: However, in ventral tissue, we found a shift towards lower receptor numbers per synapse, suggestive of smaller synapses.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative molecule counting in oscillator mice.

claim: A constant receptor density independent of synapse size was found in WT mice.
source: Consistent with our previous PALM data, we found a constant receptor density independent of synapse size in WT mice, as judged by the shallow slope of the linear regression (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of receptor density in WT mice.

claim: A similar and constant GlyR packing density was observed in synapses of oscillator mice.
source: We observed a similar and constant GlyR packing density in synapses of oscillator mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of receptor density in oscillator mice.

claim: Despite a decrease in the total number of functional GlyRs in the heterozygous oscillator mouse model, the molecular organization underlying receptor clustering within the synapse is maintained.
source: This suggests that despite a decrease in the total number of functional GlyRs in the heterozygous oscillator mouse model the molecular organization underlying receptor clustering within the synapse is maintained, in line with the lack of an overt neuromotor phenotype in these animals.
evidence: The manuscript infers the preservation of molecular organization from the constant density in oscillator mice.

claim: The receptors are assembled stereotypically in the disease model, as in WT, with synapse size consistently scaling with receptor number.
source: In other words, the receptors are assembled stereotypically in the disease model, as in WT, with synapse size consistently scaling with receptor number.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings about receptor organization in oscillator mice.

claim: Endogenous GlyRs exhibit equal receptor-scaffold occupancy at synapses across the spinal cord and throughout adulthood.
source: We show that endogenous GlyRs exhibit equal receptor-scaffold occupancy and constant packing densities of about 2000 GlyRs µm-2 at synapses across the spinal cord and throughout adulthood, even though ventral horn synapses have twice the total copy numbers, larger postsynaptic domains, and more convoluted morphologies than dorsal horn synapses.
